content: Injection can be administered through various routes, including intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, or other injectable methods. Sex workers encompass adult individuals (18 years and older) of any gender, including female, male, and transgender persons, who receive monetary or material compensation in exchange for sexual services, either on a regular or occasional basis. Community-based testing approaches include outreach initiatives such as mobile testing for general and key populations, home-based testing (door-to-door outreach), workplace testing, and testing in public venues like places of worship, parks, bars, schools, and other educational institutions. Testing campaigns are also part of this strategy. Facility-based testing involves conducting tests in healthcare settings, such as primary care clinics, inpatient wards, outpatient clinics, and specialized clinics for HIV, viral hepatitis, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and tuberculosis (TB). Testing is also performed in district, provincial, or regional hospitals, their laboratories, and private clinical services. Decentralization refers to the delegation of significant authority and resources to lower levels of the health system, including provincial, regional, district, sub-district, primary healthcare, and community levels. Differentiated service delivery is an approach that simplifies and adapts viral hepatitis services to better meet the needs of individuals living with viral hepatitis while optimizing the use of available health system resources. Integration involves the co-location and sharing of services and resources across different disease areas. For hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, this may include providing testing, prevention, care, and treatment services alongside other health services, such as HIV care, noncommunicable disease (NCD) screening, TB, STIs, antenatal care (ANC), contraceptive services, and family planning. Task-sharing involves redistributing tasks from higher-level healthcare providers to other trained cadres, such as lay providers, including community members. A lay provider is an individual trained to deliver healthcare services but who has not received formal professional or paraprofessional certification or tertiary education in healthcare. Linkage to care refers to the process of supporting individuals who test for hepatitis B or C to engage with prevention, treatment, and care services appropriate to their hepatitis status. Person-centered care focuses on organizing healthcare around the specific health needs and expectations of individuals and communities, rather than centering on diseases. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a significant public health issue and a leading cause of chronic liver disease, resulting in approximately 399,000 deaths annually. In 2019, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that 58 million people were living with chronic HCV infection, with a disproportionately high burden in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). In 2016, WHO introduced the Global Health Sector Strategy on Viral Hepatitis (2016–2021), aiming to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. Despite progress in some countries, significant gaps in testing and treatment remain. By 2019, only 21% of the 58 million individuals with chronic HCV infection had been diagnosed, and just 13% had received treatment. Achieving HCV elimination requires simplifying care pathways to address barriers to testing and treatment access. The updated guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations on priority HCV-related topics, including: Direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatment for adolescents and children aged three years and older. Simplified HCV service delivery through decentralization, integration, and task-sharing. HCV diagnostics, including point-of-care (POC) HCV RNA assays and reflex HCV RNA testing. The guidelines also incorporate updates to existing chapters, such as new protocols for using dried blood spots (DBS) for HCV RNA testing and data on detection limits for HCV RNA assays as a test of cure. The updated recommendations include: 1. Expanding DAA treatment to all individuals aged three years and older with chronic HCV infection, regardless of disease stage. 2. Simplifying service delivery by decentralizing care to lower-level facilities, integrating HCV services with existing healthcare programs, and promoting task-sharing among trained non-specialist doctors and nurses. 3. Recommending POC HCV RNA assays as an additional diagnostic approach, particularly for marginalized populations with limited healthcare access. 4. Reflex HCV RNA testing for individuals with a positive HCV antibody result to improve linkage to care and treatment. These guidelines are primarily intended for national hepatitis program managers and policymakers, particularly in LMICs, to develop national testing and treatment plans. They also serve as a reference for healthcare providers and laboratory managers involved in hepatitis care. The guidelines emphasize a public health approach, prioritizing streamlined and standardized strategies to scale up HCV services in resource-limited settings. This includes decentralization, integration, task-sharing, and empowering patients and communities. The WHO also highlights the importance of addressing stigma, discrimination, and structural barriers to healthcare, particularly for key populations such as women, adolescents, and marginalized groups. The updated guidelines align with WHO’s modular approach to updating recommendations based on emerging evidence. Future updates will consolidate all relevant guidance into a single document on the prevention, testing, care, and treatment of hepatitis B and C.
